cf.title: Per-table resync for logical replication subscriptions

input.subject: Per-table resync for logical replication subscriptions

verdict_reasoning: No objection to the goal survived: message #1 shows by test that the existing workarounds are non-local or race the apply worker. Three fixable level 2 points remain. replication-ondisk-1 is the strongest: a refresh on a forwarding node can stop a downstream apply worker. maintenance-fit-1 and standards-compat-1 concern lock-order invariants and trigger rules that only a committer who knows logical replication can accept.

brief.title: Alter subscription ... refresh table to re-copy subscribed tables
brief.problem: Postgres has no supported way to re-copy one table that a subscription already tracks. REFRESH PUBLICATION only picks up newly added tables, so operators change publication membership, which affects sibling and downstream subscribers, or edit pg_subscription_rel by hand, which races the apply worker.
brief.proposed_design: A new subscriber-local command truncates the named tables in one statement and resets their pg_subscription_rel state to init, so tablesync workers re-copy them on enable. The subscription must be disabled with no workers left, and tables another subscription also feeds are refused. The truncate WAL record carries the subscription's own origin, and mid-sync tablesync slots and then origins are dropped last.
user_visible_surface: New syntax: ALTER SUBSCRIPTION name REFRESH TABLE table_name [, ...], with no WITH options in the current version.
New errors: refused when the subscription is enabled or two_phase is on, or when another subscription populates the table.
The command fires TRUNCATE triggers as a session TRUNCATE would and needs TRUNCATE privilege on each named table.
The replicated truncate carries the subscription's origin, so origin = none downstream subscribers skip both the truncate and the re-copy.
C API: ExecuteTruncateGuts() gains an origin parameter, and truncate_check_rel/perms/activity become extern; 0002 accepts partitioned tables and partitions.
author_claims: Replaces dropping and recreating the whole subscription, which re-copies every table and loses the others' progress.
Leaves publication membership and other subscribers untouched, which the publication-membership workaround does not.
All validation runs before anything irreversible, so ordinary failures leave no changes and re-running fixes a failure in the slot drop phase.
Tagging the truncate with the subscription origin prevents data loss in two-way and origin = none cascade setups, for any cycle length.
Truncating local-only partitions matches what a replicated TRUNCATE of the root already does.
brief.thread_state: Sawada, Kuroda, Ajin Cherian, Shlok Kyal, Yilin Zhang and Song Yanli reviewed through v15; each round found lock-order deadlocks, data-loss cases or origin-state bugs, and the author fixed them. Nobody has replied to v14 or v15, and the cascade case where an intermediate node withholds TRUNCATE still leaves stale rows and apply conflicts.
unclear: No committer has commented on whether truncate-and-recopy, with the table empty during sync, is acceptable as the design.
The proposal does not say whether the enabled-subscription case will ever be supported or how.
The proposal does not show how users learn a refresh failed in the slot drop phase and must re-run it.
Nobody has confirmed that firing ordinary TRUNCATE triggers, unlike apply workers, is the wanted behaviour.
The proposal gives no plan for the intermediate node that does not publish TRUNCATE, beyond leaving stale downstream rows.

prior_attempts.title: Add `truncate` option to subscription commands
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P10 added a truncate option to existing subscription commands. This proposal adds a separate command that truncates and re-copies tables the subscription already tracks, with origin tagging, cross-subscription checks and slot cleanup.

objections.title: Refresh on a forwarding node can stop a downstream subscriber's apply worker
objections.failure_scenario: In A -> B -> C, B's publication omits truncate and C uses origin = any. An operator runs REFRESH TABLE on B, and the re-copied rows flow to C, which still holds the old rows. C logs insert_exists, its apply worker stops, and every table C subscribes to falls behind.
objections.argument: Message #28 shows the case itself: the 'withholds TRUNCATE, origin = any' row ends with C stale and its apply worker stopped. The patch documents this but neither detects nor refuses it. The command runs on B, and B can see its own publications on the table and their publish options. A local repair on one node therefore halts replication on another node, and the operator finds out only from C's server log.
objections.author_must_show: Why does the command not warn or refuse when the node republishes the table through a publication that does not publish truncate?

critic.reasoning: Message #28 confirms that C ends with insert_exists and a stopped apply worker, and v15 does not change that. B can see its own publications' publish options, so a warning or refusal is possible and nobody has decided against it.

objections.title: Command duplicates tablesync and catalog lock-order invariants with no loud failure
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes the lock level REFRESH PUBLICATION, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION or the tablesync worker takes on pg_subscription_rel, or adds a sync state. REFRESH TABLE keeps its own ordering and slot-then-origin drop sequence, so a deadlock or a lost-row case comes back. Users find out in production, through a worker killed by the deadlock detector or rows that are never copied back.
objections.argument: Each review round found a new interaction outside the command: a deadlock with a tablesync worker (#15, #16), with user transactions (#16), with partition lock order (#23), with REFRESH PUBLICATION (#29), and an origin Assert reached from triggers (#34). The fixes rest on ordering rules held in comments and TAP tests, and other subscription commands do not depend on those rules. Sawada, a committer, reviewed v3 (#9), but no committer has commented on the design since.
objections.author_must_show: Which lock-order and state-machine invariants does REFRESH TABLE depend on, and what fails at build or test time if another subscription command changes them?

critic.reasoning: Five review rounds each found a new lock-order or state interaction with another command, which supports the concern. v13 adopts the lock order of AlterSubscription_refresh() and adds a TAP assertion, but no reviewer has confirmed that this covers later changes.

objections.title: Truncate and re-copy fire different trigger sets
objections.failure_scenario: A subscriber keeps an ordinary AFTER TRUNCATE trigger and a row trigger that maintain a summary table. REFRESH TABLE fires the truncate trigger in the user's session, but the tablesync re-copy runs as replica and skips the ordinary row trigger. The summary table stays empty, and the user learns this only when reports go wrong.
objections.argument: No other ALTER SUBSCRIPTION command fires user triggers (message #33). Under v15 one operation has two halves with different trigger rules. Message #35 keeps TRUNCATE semantics and points users to ENABLE ALWAYS, but that changes how the trigger behaves for all replicated changes. Nobody has replied to that choice.
objections.author_must_show: Why should one command fire the session's TRUNCATE triggers for the discard but only replica or always triggers for the refill, and not one rule for both halves?

critic.reasoning: Message #33 asked which trigger rule applies, and message #35 kept session TRUNCATE semantics with no reviewer reply. The scenario is weak, because ordinary row triggers never fire for replicated rows on a subscriber, but the consistency question stays open.

refuted.title: Origin-tagged truncate breaks downstream nodes that do not publish TRUNCATE
refuted.failure_scenario: In A->B->C, B's publication uses publish = 'insert, update, delete'. An operator runs REFRESH TABLE on B. C never receives the truncate but does receive the re-copied rows, logs insert_exists, and its apply worker stops. The operator finds out from C's log, possibly hours later.
refuted.argument: The author's own matrix in message #28 shows this row as "stale" with the apply worker stopped, and v15 leaves it unchanged. Kuroda raised it in message #27. The command quietly depends on a setting on another node that the operator may not connect to this repair. The documentation does not warn about it or offer a refusal path.
refuted.author_must_show: What should REFRESH TABLE do, warn or refuse, when the table is in a local publication that does not publish truncate but does publish inserts?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. The title also blames the origin tag, but the matrix in message #28 shows the same stale result in v11, before the tag existed.

refuted.title: Refreshing a partitioned root discards local-only partitions
refuted.failure_scenario: A subscriber keeps locally generated rows in tab_part2 under a replicated root, and the publication excludes truncate, so those rows have always survived. The operator runs REFRESH TABLE tab to fix tab_part1, and the local rows are lost with no way back.
refuted.argument: Message #25 and the 0002 commit message justify this as matching a replicated TRUNCATE of the root. That comparison holds only when the publisher truncates and publishes truncate, and this setup opted out of both. A repair command that destroys data outside what the publisher can restore is a different contract from what the user configured, even with the documentation warning.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should REFRESH TABLE on a root truncate a partition that the publisher never populates, when the subscription's own publication would never have truncated it?

critic.reasoning: The 0002 documentation states that subscriber-only partitions are truncated and not refilled. The re-copy routes rows by the subscriber's partition bounds, so the command cannot tell which partitions the publisher never fills, and the user names the root explicitly.

refuted.title: Partial failure during slot drops leaves a mid-sync table unable to resume
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator refreshes a table parked in FINISHEDCOPY, and the publisher connection drops after its tablesync slot is gone. The transaction rolls back to FINISHEDCOPY with no slot behind it. On enable, the tablesync worker repeats 'replication slot ... does not exist' until someone re-runs the command.
refuted.argument: Message #28 reproduces this and settles on documenting re-run as the remedy. That copies what DROP SUBSCRIPTION and REFRESH PUBLICATION do, but those commands do not leave a catalog row pointing at a slot that no longer exists. Here the rolled-back pg_subscription_rel state refers to a dropped remote slot. The only signal is a repeating worker error, which the brief also lists as open.
refuted.author_must_show: Can a failed run leave the affected relations in a state the tablesync worker handles itself, or else report which relations need the command run again?

critic.reasoning: The command returns an error to the client when a slot drop fails, and message #28 documents re-running as the remedy. REFRESH PUBLICATION and DROP SUBSCRIPTION also drop tablesync slots last with missing_ok, so a rollback there restores rows for dropped slots too.

refuted.title: User backend writing WAL under a subscription origin widens what origins mean
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension or a later conflict-detection feature assumes that WAL tagged with a subscription origin came from that subscription's apply process. A REFRESH TABLE truncate breaks that assumption, and the error appears only in cascade or two-way setups. Extensions that call ExecuteTruncateGuts() stop compiling when the new parameter lands.
refuted.argument: Until now, only apply workers and sessions that set up an origin explicitly write origin-tagged WAL. v14 adds an origin parameter to ExecuteTruncateGuts() and makes three truncate_check functions extern, and only this command uses them (#35, commit message). The v13 attempt to set the origin across the whole truncate crashed in three ways (#34, #35), so the narrow placement is an invariant that later changes to truncate code must keep.
refuted.author_must_show: Is a per-record origin argument on ExecuteTruncateGuts() a mechanism other callers would use, and where is the rule documented that only the WAL record carries it?

critic.reasoning: Any session can already write WAL under an origin through pg_replication_origin_session_setup(), so the assumed guarantee does not exist today. A changed C signature in a major release is normal, and the parameter itself limits the origin to the WAL record.

refuted.title: Visible semantics are fixed before the enabled or concurrent design exists
refuted.failure_scenario: Users build runbooks around REFRESH TABLE: the table is empty during the sync, user TRUNCATE triggers fire, and a truncate goes downstream under the subscription origin. A later version that copies into a new relfilenode or works on enabled subscriptions has to keep these behaviours or change them. Downstream nodes that withhold TRUNCATE already get stale rows and a stopped apply worker.
refuted.argument: The author names a relfilenode swap as the natural follow-up (#13) and leaves the enabled-subscription case open (#1, #2). The trigger behaviour was questioned in #33 and kept without a decision from others (#35). The withheld-TRUNCATE cascade still ends in insert_exists conflicts (#28).
refuted.author_must_show: Which behaviours of REFRESH TABLE (an empty table during the sync, trigger firing, propagation of the truncate) would a future concurrent or enabled-subscription version keep, and which would it change?

critic.reasoning: The scenario names no behaviour that a later enabled or concurrent version could not relax, since lifting a restriction breaks no runbook. Its concrete parts repeat standards-compat-1 and replication-ondisk-1.

refuted.title: Demand rests on one operator's topology, with no field reports
refuted.failure_scenario: The project adds a command whose correctness needed fifteen revisions of locking, origin and trigger fixes. Few users run diverged subscriber tables in fan-out or forwarding setups, so later regressions in this path go unreported until a rare user loses rows.
refuted.argument: The only demand shown is the author's own use cases in message #1: an inconsistent table, a changed row filter, and a forwarder repair. The thread cites no -general or -bugs reports and no second user who needs it, and does not say how other systems handle it. Reviewers in messages #9 to #34 tested the design but did not report needing it. Sawada's engagement and the REFRESH SEQUENCES analogy in messages #3 and #4 lower this concern without settling it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users besides this deployment hit diverged or stuck subscribed tables, how often, and what did they do instead, for example drop and recreate the subscription?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 shows by test that the publication workaround wipes the downstream node and leaves the sibling behind, and that the catalog edit races the apply worker. Core has REFRESH SEQUENCES for the same need, and pglogical ships a per-table resynchronize function.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The truncate WAL record carries the subscription's origin, and the command drops tablesync slots and origins.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The command resets pg_subscription_rel rows to init from a user backend; it adds no catalog column.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: ExecuteTruncateGuts() gains an origin parameter, and three truncate_check functions become extern.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: New ALTER SUBSCRIPTION name REFRESH TABLE table_name [, ...] syntax in gram.y.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: The patch adds tab completion in src/bin/psql/tab-complete.in.c.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The command needs TRUNCATE privilege on each table and fires TRUNCATE triggers in the caller's session.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The command keeps its own lock order and slot-then-origin drop sequence next to tablesync and REFRESH PUBLICATION.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Should REFRESH TABLE warn or refuse when the node republishes the table through a publication that publishes inserts but not truncate?
Which lock-order and sync-state invariants does REFRESH TABLE depend on, and which test fails if another subscription command changes them?
Why does the discard fire the session's TRUNCATE triggers while the re-copy fires only replica or always triggers, instead of one rule for both?
Would a later enabled-subscription version keep truncate-and-recopy with the table empty during sync, or use a different mechanism?

committability.owner_note: Masahiko Sawada is the CommitFest reviewer and reviewed early versions, but nobody has replied to v14 or v15. The owner must know tablesync, replication origins and truncate.
committability.liability: The owner signs for lock ordering against tablesync workers, REFRESH PUBLICATION and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION, for origin-tagged truncate WAL in cascade setups, and for the trigger behaviour, for as long as the command exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author fixed every reported problem through fifteen versions and rebased twice after CFbot reports, which suggests continued follow-up.

priority.reason: The need is shown by test in message #1 and the author responds to review. The two patches total about 135 KiB across subscriptioncmds.c, tablecmds.c and worker.c, and each review round found a new lock-order or origin problem.

provisional_note: The lock order, the slot-then-origin drop sequence and the placement of the origin on the truncate WAL record could not be checked without the code. Only 3 of 36 messages were read directly, so later discussion is known only through the objections.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Warning for Datatype mismatch between subscriber table and publisher table for logical replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes logical replication emit a warning when a subscriber table column has a different data type from the matching publisher column. The goal is to show type mismatches early so users can debug replication problems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not revise the patch after review, and it had not passed CI since about mid March, so the CF entry was closed. Ashutosh Bapat had asked for the unrelated file renames to be removed. He also noted that the code maps columns by position, and that it compares type OIDs and names on the subscriber without using the remote type cache.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since this has not been fixed, and the patch has not passed CI since at least
mid March, I'll close this CF entry.

precedents_retrieved.title: transaction statistics of logical replication subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed counting failed transactions and their sizes in pg_stat_replication_slots, so that users could tell successful logical decoding from repeated failed attempts. By the last version, the patch instead added apply_commit_count and apply_rollback_count columns to pg_stat_subscription_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila noted that pg_stat_database already shows committed and rolled-back transactions per database, so the new counters largely duplicate it, and he asked whether anyone saw value in them. Masahiko Sawada agreed that commit and rollback counts without transaction sizes no longer meet the original goal and have no concrete use case. The author then marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I’m concerned that adding only apply_commit_count
and apply_rollback_count ends up adding the duplicate statistics with
no concrete use cases.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reuse Workers and Replication Slots during Logical Replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a tablesync worker, after it finishes one table, pick up the next table in init state and sync it, keeping its replication slot. This removes the cost of starting a new worker and creating and dropping a slot for each table, which matters most for many empty or small tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks by reviewers showed regressions in some settings, and the v28 design #2 results were up to about twice as slow as HEAD and varied widely between runs. The patch also no longer applied to HEAD. Amit Kapila proposed Returned with feedback because the regressions still needed analysis, and vignesh C asked for a new entry with a fix for the regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IIRC, there were some regressions observed with this patch. So, one
needs to analyze those as well.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix alter subscription concurrency errors
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Amit Kapila, Alvaro Herrera, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixed "tuple concurrently updated" errors from concurrent ALTER/DROP SUBSCRIPTION statements on the same subscription by re-fetching the subscription tuple after acquiring its lock, using a retry loop modeled on dbcommands.c. A later version also allowed ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... OWNER TO to run concurrently with the other subscription commands.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected that adding lock-and-retry lookup code specific to subscriptions does not scale, since the same problem affects other object types. Alvaro Herrera suggested using get_object_address() instead, and Tom Lane added that this might first require improving its error reporting. The author did not post an updated version for several commitfests. He then said his own test-flakiness problem had been worked around and that he was not motivated to address the issue for all DDL commands, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think the patch as-submitted is pretty uninteresting, mainly because the
design of adding bespoke lock code for subscription objects doesn't scale.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow single table VACUUM in transaction block
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Greg Stark, Robert Haas, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch let VACUUM on a single table run inside a transaction block, so scripts run with --single-transaction would not fail; it skipped PROC_IN_VACUUM and the datfrozenxid update in that case. Later versions forced VACUUM FULL for temp tables and queued an autovacuum request for other tables, and finally added an explicit VACUUM (BACKGROUND) option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to a VACUUM command that runs in-process in some cases and as a background autovacuum request in others. Robert Haas and Tom Lane also rejected making background vacuum the default or controlling it with a GUC, because users would notice the delay and regression tests expect VACUUM to finish at once. The author agreed, switched to an explicit VACUUM (BACKGROUND) option, and proposed returning this entry and opening a new one for that design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Basically, I am not buying Simon's requirement that this be transparent.

precedents_retrieved.title: Bug in ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER / ... CONNECTION with broken old server
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER / ... CONNECTION (and DROP SUBSCRIPTION) failing when the subscription's old foreign server is broken, for example after its user mapping was dropped. GetSubscription() would build the old server's connection string only when it is needed. A later part (0003) would wrap conninfo construction in a subtransaction so that DROP SUBSCRIPTION can absorb errors such as a missing user mapping and report them with a hint.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The core fix was not rejected: Jeff Davis committed parts 0001 and 0002. The remaining part, 0003, was dropped because absorbing every error that might occur inside the FDW connection was judged inappropriate, and Amit Kapila questioned whether the proposed hint addressed the reported problem. Jeff Davis closed the open item and treated the remaining DROP SUBSCRIPTION issue with tablesync slots and slot_name=NONE as a separate pre-existing bug.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: For 0003, I don't think we can absorb every kind of error that might happen inside fdwconnection.

precedents_retrieved.title: tablesync early exit
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a tablesync worker call process_syncing_tables() before it enters the apply main loop, so a worker with nothing left to do exits early. The author presented it as a small optimization and as a cleaner split of work between tablesync and apply workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila objected that exiting before the tablesync worker receives any message skips changes up to the LSN where the copy finished. That is safe with the current code but would lose changes for the table in a design where the apply worker applies streamed in-progress transactions, which had already been proposed on -hackers. The saving was only the work to receive messages for one transaction, so the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As per my understanding, this is safe as per the current code but it
can't be guaranteed for future implementations and the amount of extra
work is additional work to receive the messages for one transaction.

precedents_retrieved.title: Synchronize logical replication slots from primary to standby
precedents_retrieved.summary: A background worker on a physical standby periodically fetches logical replication slot information from the primary, so that after failover a logical subscriber finds up-to-date slots on the new primary. Later versions added synchronize_slot_names on the standby to pick which slots to sync, and standby_slot_names on the primary to hold logical replication back until the listed physical standbys catch up.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund found that the patch breaks the catalog_xmin guarantee: row versions still needed for logical decoding on the standby can be removed. He said it needs a mechanism such as the "Minimal logical decoding on standbys" patch, which the author said was not near ready. Reviewers also objected to the blocking wait and the per-commit work added to reorderbuffer.c, and to the worker-per-database design tied to the logical replication launcher. The author listed these and an open configuration design as significant jobs still to do.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The patch as-is just breaks one of the fundamental guarantees necessary for logical decoding, that no rows versions can be removed that are still required for logical decoding (signalled via catalog_xmin).

roaster_notes.note: Only [P10] is close, and it was withdrawn with no recorded reason, so no earlier objection can be tested against this design. [P23] concerns TRUNCATE under session_replication_role = replica and also has no recorded reason. Within the thread, message #1 and message #3 point only to the REFRESH SEQUENCES syntax debate, which supports the chosen spelling.
The REFRESH TABLE spelling follows REFRESH SEQUENCES and was agreed in messages #3 and #4. It adds no keyword, GUC or catalog object, so pg_dump and psql conventions are not affected.

The proposal adds no new WAL record type, catalog column or on-disk format, so physical standbys and pg_upgrade are not affected. The ExecuteTruncateGuts() signature change targets master only and is a normal major-version API change.

No security objection survives. Running the command takes subscription ownership plus TRUNCATE on each table, rechecked under AccessExclusiveLock. Triggers fire as in a TRUNCATE in that session. The origin-tagged truncate gives a subscription owner nothing the subscription's own apply could not already write under that origin.
Objections were found. Hot-path cost is not one of them, because the work runs only when a user runs the command.

Postgres has no supported way to re-copy one already-subscribed table at a slot-consistent point. REFRESH PUBLICATION skips tracked tables, REFRESH SEQUENCES covers only sequences, and the publication-membership and pg_subscription_rel workarounds are non-local or race the apply worker, as message #1 shows. A manual COPY cannot line up with the apply position, and no extension or hook does this job, so the angle finds the need unmet. [P10] has no recorded reason and was not used.
Demand is plausible: the workarounds in message #1 are shown to be non-local, and a committer is engaged. So this is a request to show demand, not a rejection.
